message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Properties**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | H‑1 (protium), H‑2 (deuterium), H‑3 (tritium) |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV (first) |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV (negative, meaning it does not readily accept an electron) |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Atomic radius | ~31 pm (covalent) |
| | Van der Waals radius | ~120 pm |
| **Physical State (298 K, 1 atm)** | State | Gas |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (−423.17 °F) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (−434.69 °F) |
| | Density | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (≈0.00008988 g cm⁻³) |
| | Molar volume | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Specific heat (Cp) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Heat of vaporization | 0.449 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Speed of sound | ~1270 m s⁻¹ (in pure H₂ at 300 K) |
| | Refractive index | 1.000132 (at 589 nm) |
| | Dielectric constant | 1.000132 (static) |
| | Viscosity | 8.76 µPa·s (at 300 K) |
| | Thermal conductivity | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| **Chemical Properties** | Oxidation states | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride), 0 (H₂) |
| | Bonding | Forms covalent bonds; H₂ is a diatomic molecule with a single σ bond |
| | Reactivity | Highly reactive with many elements; forms hydrides with metals, acids with nonmetals |
| | Acid–base behavior | Acts as a weak acid (H⁺ donor) in aqueous solution; forms hydronium (H₃O⁺) |
| | Redox behavior | Strong reducing agent (especially in the form of H₂ gas or hydride ions) |
| | Combustion | Combines with O₂ → 2 H₂O (exothermic, ΔH ≈ –286 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Hydrogen bonding | H₂ itself does not form hydrogen bonds; however, H atoms in molecules like water, alcohols, etc., can participate in H‑bonding |
| | Solubility in water | ~1.6 g L⁻¹ at 25 °C (≈0.0009 mol L⁻¹) |
| | Solubility in organic solvents | Variable; generally soluble in nonpolar solvents (e.g., hexane) |
| | Spectroscopic features | 1s→2p transition (Lyman series) in UV; rotational/vibrational transitions in IR (stretching frequency ≈ 4401 cm⁻¹) |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Protium (¹H) | Stable, most abundant |
| | Deuterium (²H) | Stable, 0.015% natural abundance |
| | Tritium (³H) | Radioactive (half‑life ≈ 12.32 y), used in nuclear fusion and radiolabeling |
| **Astrophysical & Industrial Notes** | Stellar fusion | Proton–proton chain (H + H → D + e⁺ + νₑ) powers main‑sequence stars |
| | Fusion fuel | Deuterium–tritium (D–T) reaction releases 17.6 MeV per reaction |
| | Industrial use | Hydrogenation, ammonia synthesis (Haber–Bosch), fuel cells, metal processing |
| | Safety | Extremely flammable; forms explosive mixtures with air (4–75 % H₂ in air) |
| | Storage | Cryogenic liquid (–253 °C), high‑pressure gas cylinders, metal hydrides, chemical carriers (e.g., ammonia borane) |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Lightest element**: atomic number 1, mass ~1 u, extremely low density.
- **Highly reactive**: forms hydrides with metals, reacts with nonmetals, combusts readily.
- **Key role in energy**: fuels hydrogen‑based fuel cells, fuels nuclear fusion (D–T).
- **Isotopic diversity**: stable protium, stable deuterium, radioactive tritium.
- **Physical extremes**: very low boiling/melting points, high speed of sound, low viscosity.

Feel free to ask for deeper details on any specific property or application!
